claim: Black academics and other scholars with marginalized identities are awarded tenure at lower rates than their white colleagues.
source: This power has an outsized impact on Black academics and other scholars with marginalized identities, who are awarded tenure at lower rates than their white colleagues.
evidence: Supported by citations to scholarly literature on tenure disparities

claim: Black scholars are promoted with tenure at a lower rate than their white colleagues.
source: Black scholars, already severely underrepresented as junior faculty, are promoted with tenure at a lower rate than their white colleagues (Frazier, 2011; Herbert, 2012; Stewart, 2012; US Department of Education, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on tenure promotion rates

claim: Black scholars have had to overcome more hurdles than their white colleagues to become assistant professors.
source: If anything, Black scholars have had to overcome more hurdles than their white colleagues to become assistant professors (Diep, 2020; Frazier, 2011), surviving and excelling in long and unforgiving training and selection processes that are biased against them.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on barriers faced by Black scholars

claim: Lower tenure rates for Black scholars are primarily due to a narrow definition of 'excellence' that encompasses only some forms of contribution to academia.
source: We believe this is primarily due to two factors that tenure letter writers can intentionally work to overturn: (i) a narrow definition of 'excellence' that encompasses only some forms of contribution to academia
evidence: Based on the authors' inference from the literature and their analysis

claim: Lower tenure rates for Black scholars are due to unrecognized invisible burdens of mentoring and representation that fall disproportionately on Black faculty.
source: We believe this is primarily due to two factors that tenure letter writers can intentionally work to overturn: (i) a narrow definition of 'excellence' that encompasses only some forms of contribution to academia, and (ii) the unrecognized invisible burdens of mentoring and representation that fall disproportionately on the shoulders of Black faculty (and more so on Black women, who hold doubly marginalized, intersectional identities).
evidence: Based on the authors' inference from the literature and their analysis

claim: Black women faculty face disproportionate burdens due to doubly marginalized, intersectional identities.
source: the unrecognized invisible burdens of mentoring and representation that fall disproportionately on the shoulders of Black faculty (and more so on Black women, who hold doubly marginalized, intersectional identities).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about intersectionality and marginalization

claim: Anti-Black racism imposes myriad, interacting harms on Black scholars in US academia.
source: Throughout, we will refer specifically to Black faculty, as we are writing from a US-centric vantage point on academia, where anti-Black racism imposes myriad, interacting harms on Black scholars (Bell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bell et al., 2021

claim: The issues and recommendations discussed apply to indigenous scholars, scholars of Color, LGBTQ+ scholars, scholars with disabilities, first-generation scholars, scholars from low-income backgrounds, and women in most academic fields.
source: However, the issues we discuss and recommendations we make apply to indigenous scholars, scholars of Color, LGBTQ+ scholars, scholars with disabilities, first-generation scholars, scholars from low-income backgrounds, and, in most academic fields, also women.
evidence: Based on the authors' inference about the applicability of their recommendations

claim: The recommendations do not 'lower the bar' of tenure standards in academia.
source: We emphasize that our recommendations by no means 'lower the bar' of tenure standards in academia.
evidence: Authors' assertion about the nature of their recommendations

claim: Recognizing the full ways that historically excluded scholars excel can help raise the standards across academia.
source: To the contrary, recognizing the full ways that historically excluded scholars excel and help create an excellent academic culture can help raise the standards across academia.
evidence: Authors' inference about the impact of their recommendations

claim: The academic profession was developed to have strict boundaries about who is allowed to be a part of the profession and what work is valued.
source: The academic profession was developed to have strict boundaries about who is allowed to be a part of the profession and what work is valued.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the history of academia

claim: Objectivity, linearity, generalizability, and detachment have long been the standard for evaluating academic rigor.
source: Certain values and qualities (such as objectivity, linearity, generalizability, and detachment) have long been the standard for evaluating academic rigor and granting membership into this highly selective profession (Gonzales, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzales, 2018

claim: Black scholars engaging in community-focused research and racial justice work are often evaluated negatively because their work is viewed as not being objective and their advocacy is viewed as problematic.
source: Thus, Black scholars engaging in community-focused research and racial justice work are often evaluated negatively because their work is viewed as not being objective and their advocacy is viewed as problematic (Gonzales, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzales, 2018

claim: Black scholars are overrepresented in topics related to racial discrimination and African studies.
source: Indeed, Black scholars are overrepresented in topics related to racial discrimination and African studies, but often cited less than scholars from other groups (Kozlowski et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kozlowski et al., 2022

claim: Black scholars are often cited less than scholars from other groups.
source: Indeed, Black scholars are overrepresented in topics related to racial discrimination and African studies, but often cited less than scholars from other groups (Kozlowski et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kozlowski et al., 2022

claim: Black scholars' research is often undervalued by evaluators embedded in 'white supremacy culture'.
source: Therefore, in evaluation processes, like tenure and promotion, their research is often undervalued by evaluators embedded in what Dr. Tema Okun describes as 'white supremacy culture' (Okun, 1999; Okun, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okun's work on white supremacy culture

claim: White supremacy culture is the widespread ideology baked into the beliefs, values, norms, and standards of groups, communities, and institutions, teaching that whiteness holds value.
source: According to Okun, "White supremacy culture is the widespread ideology baked into the beliefs, values, norms, and standards of our groups (many if not most of them), our communities, our towns, our states, our nation, teaching us both overtly and covertly that whiteness holds value, whiteness is value" (https://www.whitesupremacyculture.info/what-is-it.html).
evidence: Direct quote from Okun's work defining white supremacy culture

claim: Academic culture is steeped in the beliefs and values associated with 'white supremacy culture'.
source: Whether we are aware of it or not, academic culture is steeped in the beliefs and values Okun associates with 'white supremacy culture'
evidence: Authors' inference based on Okun's framework

claim: The values of white supremacy culture are not a necessity in academia.
source: These values are not a necessity in academia.
evidence: Authors' assertion about the contingent nature of academic values

claim: Most academics trained in academic culture may not recognize the invisible 'rules of the game' despite the fact that these rules limit creativity and inclusion.
source: Most of us, having been trained in this culture for years, may not even recognize these invisible but ever-present 'rules of the game' despite the fact that these rules limit creativity and inclusion.
evidence: Authors' inference about the implicit nature of academic cultural norms

claim: Academia's embodiment of 'white supremacy culture' diminishes the learning environment in institutions.
source: Academia's embodiment of 'white supremacy culture' diminishes the learning environment in our institutions, limits vital representation of Black scholars and their scholarship, and harms Black faculty wellness and opportunities for advancement (Davis, 2021; Diep, 2020; Mosley et al., 2021; Bell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on harms to Black faculty

claim: Academia's embodiment of 'white supremacy culture' limits vital representation of Black scholars and their scholarship.
source: Academia's embodiment of 'white supremacy culture' diminishes the learning environment in our institutions, limits vital representation of Black scholars and their scholarship, and harms Black faculty wellness and opportunities for advancement (Davis, 2021; Diep, 2020; Mosley et al., 2021; Bell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on harms to Black faculty

claim: Academia's embodiment of 'white supremacy culture' harms Black faculty wellness and opportunities for advancement.
source: Academia's embodiment of 'white supremacy culture' diminishes the learning environment in our institutions, limits vital representation of Black scholars and their scholarship, and harms Black faculty wellness and opportunities for advancement (Davis, 2021; Diep, 2020; Mosley et al., 2021; Bell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on harms to Black faculty

claim: Harms from white supremacy culture pervade all aspects of academia and are particularly well-documented for the tenure and promotion process.
source: These harms pervade all aspects of academia and are particularly well-documented for the tenure and promotion process (Frazier, 2011; Jones et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to research on tenure and promotion

claim: Examples of harms in tenure and promotion include lack of recognition for increased service load.
source: where examples include lack of recognition for increased service load (Gewin, 2020; Guarino and Borden, 2017; Hirshfield and Joseph, 2012; Jimenez et al., 2019; McCluney and Rabelo, 2019; Moore, 2017, Social Sciences Feminist Network Research Interest Group, 2017)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on service load disparities

claim: Examples of harms in tenure and promotion include marginalization of research.
source: where examples include lack of recognition for increased service load (Gewin, 2020; Guarino and Borden, 2017; Hirshfield and Joseph, 2012; Jimenez et al., 2019; McCluney and Rabelo, 2019; Moore, 2017, Social Sciences Feminist Network Research Interest Group, 2017), marginalization of research (Padilla, 1994; Settles et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to research on research marginalization

claim: Examples of harms in tenure and promotion include lower rates of publication and funding.
source: where examples include lack of recognition for increased service load (Gewin, 2020; Guarino and Borden, 2017; Hirshfield and Joseph, 2012; Jimenez et al., 2019; McCluney and Rabelo, 2019; Moore, 2017, Social Sciences Feminist Network Research Interest Group, 2017), marginalization of research (Padilla, 1994; Settles et al., 2022), and lower rates of publication and funding (Taffe and Gilpin, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to research on publication and funding disparities

claim: Critical reforms to address racial inequities in tenure have been identified.
source: While critical reforms have been identified (e.g., Roadmap for Racial Equity at UNC Chapel Hill)
evidence: Reference to specific reform document

claim: Some institutions such as Indiana University–Purdue University Indianapolis and University of Oregon are pursuing structural remedies to tenure inequities.
source: and some institutions – such as, Indiana University–Purdue University Indianapolis and University of Oregon – are pursuing structural remedies to some of these problems (Truong, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Truong, 2021

claim: Many scholars who wish to support anti-racist reforms of academia are unable to individually effect such changes in their institutions.
source: many scholars who wish to support anti-racist reforms of academia are unable to individually effect such changes in their institutions.
evidence: Authors' inference about the limitations of individual power

claim: Scholars who have successfully navigated the tenure process likely still lack the power to change the policies and procedures that harm Black scholars.
source: Indeed, even scholars who have successfully navigated the tenure process and hold relatively powerful positions in their institutions and disciplines likely still lack the power to change the policies and procedures that harm Black scholars.
evidence: Authors' inference about institutional power structures

claim: Successful scholars are regularly asked to serve as external evaluators in the tenure process at peer institutions.
source: However, such successful scholars are regularly asked to serve as external evaluators in the tenure process at peer institutions
evidence: Based on established knowledge about tenure processes

claim: Individual scholars committed to anti-racism can have a substantial impact on the career trajectories of Black scholars through the external evaluation process.
source: and it is in this process that individual scholars committed to anti-racism and to an expansive and inclusive academic culture can have a substantial impact on the career trajectories of Black scholars.
evidence: Authors' inference about the potential impact of anti-racist letter writing

claim: Writing tenure/promotion letters is an excellent opportunity to push back against traditional, narrow criteria for promotion and toward a more holistic view of scholarly contributions.
source: Writing tenure/promotion letters is an excellent opportunity to push back against traditional, narrow criteria for promotion and toward a more holistic view of scholarly contributions (for example, see Renwick et al., 2020).
evidence: Authors' assertion with supporting citation

claim: Previous guidelines for writing tenure and promotion letters often embrace and perpetuate an academic culture focused on a traditional, narrow understanding of scholarship.
source: Although previous guidelines for writing tenure and promotion letters have been proposed (Goldman, 2016; Goldman, 2017; Kong et al., 2021; Strassman, 2016; Female Science Professor, 2014), they often embrace and perpetuate an academic culture focused on a traditional, narrow understanding of scholarship.
evidence: Authors' critique of existing guidelines with citations

claim: Writing a tenure letter purely from one's own lived experience and expectations can inadvertently introduce bias and undermine the success of the candidate.
source: Writing a tenure letter purely from one's own lived experience and expectations can also inadvertently introduce bias and undermine the success of the candidate, as most letter writers have not experienced academia as a racially marginalized scholar.
evidence: Authors' inference about the risks of uncritical letter writing

claim: Most letter writers have not experienced academia as a racially marginalized scholar.
source: as most letter writers have not experienced academia as a racially marginalized scholar.
evidence: Based on knowledge about the demographics of senior faculty

claim: The current system is a vicious positive feedback cycle where letters written by the majority of faculty reify the current culture.
source: The current system is a vicious positive feedback cycle: letters written by the majority of faculty (i.e., based on the tacitly accepted values of white men) reify the current culture and squander the opportunity to intentionally recognize its limitations and expand beyond it.
evidence: Authors' inference about the self-perpetuating nature of bias

claim: The authors are a group of mostly non-Black academics in STEM fields, most of them women.
source: We are a group of mostly non-Black academics in STEM fields, most of us women, who are learning about and working toward Black liberation in academia.
evidence: Authors' self-description of their identities

claim: The authors participated in the 2020 and 2021 'Academics for Black Survival and Wellness (A4BL)' courses.
source: We participated in the 2020 and 2021 "Academics for Black Survival and Wellness (A4BL)" courses envisioned and implemented by Dr. Della Mosley and Pearis Bellamy, with shared wisdom from a large number of anti-Black-racism scholars.
evidence: Authors' statement about their training

claim: The set of recommendations arose from a working group formed during the 2021 A4BL course.
source: This set of recommendations arose from a working group formed during the 2021 course.
evidence: Authors' statement about the origin of their recommendations

claim: The project represents an incremental challenge to a system in urgent need of major transformations regarding diversity, equity, and inclusion.
source: We recognize that our project represents an incremental challenge to a system in urgent need of major transformations regarding diversity, equity, and inclusion.
evidence: Authors' acknowledgment of the limitations of their approach

claim: The recommendations are based on coursework, literature on racial and gender bias and equity, and the authors' experiences as largely tenured faculty.
source: We therefore offer these recommendations that are based on what we learned from the above coursework, literature on racial and gender bias and equity, and our experiences as largely tenured faculty who are regularly in a position to evaluate fellow scholars.
evidence: Authors' statement about the basis for their recommendations

claim: The recommendations are inspired by the work of Bell et al., 2021, Berhe and Kim, 2019a; Berhe and Kim, 2019b, The University of Arizona Commission on the Status of Women, 2016, Okun, 2021 and Itchuaqiyaq and Walton, 2021.
source: These recommendations are inspired by the work of Bell et al., 2021, Berhe and Kim, 2019a; Berhe and Kim, 2019b, The University of Arizona Commission on the Status of Women, 2016, Okun, 2021 and Itchuaqiyaq and Walton, 2021.
evidence: Authors' acknowledgment of their sources

claim: The act of being called to review is also a call to power.
source: Itchuaqiyaq and Walton, 2021 rightly point out that the "act of being called to review is also a call to power".
evidence: Citation to Itchuaqiyaq and Walton, 2021

claim: The power of writing tenure review letters comes with a responsibility to hold oneself and other power-holders accountable for anti-Black racism.
source: This is doubly true for tenure review letters, and with that power comes a responsibility to hold both oneself and other power-holders (e.g., letter requesters, evaluation committees) accountable for anti-Black racism and to support the success of marginalized scholars.
evidence: Authors' inference about the ethical responsibilities of letter writers

claim: The recommendations apply more widely to other marginalized scholars and to letter writers of all identities.
source: Here, we provide recommendations for non-Black academics writing letters for Black candidates; however, we believe that these recommendations apply more widely, both to other marginalized scholars and to letter writers of all identities.
evidence: Authors' assertion about the broader applicability of their recommendations

claim: The list of recommendations incorporates feedback and reflects substantial contributions from other attendees and leaders of the 2021 Academics for Black Survival and Wellness training.
source: The list of recommendations incorporates feedback and reflects substantial contributions from other attendees and leaders of the 2021 Academics for Black Survival and Wellness training and from a diverse group of scholars in our professional networks.
evidence: Authors' statement about the collaborative development of recommendations

claim: Recommendations for critical awareness and intentionality are important even when requested only to evaluate a candidate's scholarship.
source: We emphasize that these recommendations for critical awareness and intentionality are important even when requested only to evaluate a candidate's scholarship
evidence: Authors' assertion about the scope of their recommendations

claim: Recommendations are especially important the more marginalized intersecting identities the candidate holds.
source: and are especially important the more marginalized intersecting identities the candidate holds.
evidence: Authors' inference about the importance of intersectionality

claim: Letter writers should reflect on their various identities and background, including gender, race, class, sexual orientation, able-bodiedness, culture, ethnicity, religion and nationality.
source: First, we encourage you to reflect on your various identities and background, including gender, race, class, sexual orientation, able-bodiedness, culture, ethnicity, religion and nationality.
evidence: Authors' recommendation for self-reflection

claim: White scholars writing letters for Black scholars should consider their own racial identity development.
source: If you are a white scholar writing a letter for a Black scholar, consider your own racial identity development (see Helms, 2020) and engage with scaffolded anti-racist resources as needed (Stamborski et al., 2020).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with supporting citations

claim: Letter writers should ask the person who requested the letter about the make-up and perspective of the department and institution.
source: Second, in order to gather relevant information and to encourage reflection on the part of the institution you are writing for, ask the person who requested the letter (e.g., the department chair) about the make-up and perspective of the department and institution (Figure 1 top, box 2).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Letter writers should research the candidate's CV, professional website, and public-facing social media to learn more about their influential work inside and outside of academia.
source: As a final preparatory step (Figure 1 top, box 3), research the candidate's CV, professional website, and public-facing social media to learn more about their influential work inside and outside of academia (e.g., DEI work, collaborative work, leadership).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Letter writers should include a positionality statement or other description of their own backgrounds and experiences.
source: Like we did in this paper, we suggest you include a positionality statement (see Clemons, 2019; UCLA Library, 2021a; UCLA Library, 2021b; Taylor Institute, 2022; Derry, 2017; Darwin Holmes, 2020; Lacy, 2017) or other description of your own backgrounds and experiences and how they shape how you are evaluating the candidate (Figure 1 middle, box 1).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with supporting citations and reference to Figure 1

claim: Letter writers should use 'I' statements that clarify the subjectivity of their assessments.
source: Throughout, we recommend you use "I" statements that clarify the subjectivity of your assessments.
evidence: Authors' recommendation for writing style

claim: All assessment is subjective.
source: While all assessment is subjective, an 'objective' meritocracy is a tantalizing illusion that is pervasive in academia.
evidence: Authors' assertion about the nature of assessment

claim: An 'objective' meritocracy is a tantalizing illusion that is pervasive in academia.
source: While all assessment is subjective, an 'objective' meritocracy is a tantalizing illusion that is pervasive in academia.
evidence: Authors' critique of academic culture

claim: Letter writers should use language that amplifies the candidate's formal title or position rather than language that can detract from their credibility.
source: In referring to the candidate, use language that amplifies their formal title or position (e.g., "Assistant Professor") rather than language that can detract from their credibility (e.g., "junior scholar," "early-career").
evidence: Authors' recommendation for respectful language

claim: Letter writers should use 'Dr.' or another appropriate title rather than a first name when referring to the candidate.
source: Throughout, we recommend you use "Dr." or another appropriate title rather than a first name (Figure 1 middle, box 2)
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Letter writers should name all of the candidate's accomplishments, including non-traditional scholarship.
source: Here, it is vitally important that you name all of the candidate's accomplishments (Figure 1 middle, box 3). That is, in addition to mentioning traditional scholarship (papers, books, citations, invited talks, grants), you can expand your own – and the readers' – notion of what a scholarly accomplishment is.
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Letter writers should call attention to grant applications submitted, symposia organized, spaces and classes created, leadership and service, education of the community, creation of public policy, impact on public health, and participation in public relations or recruiting efforts.
source: For example, you should call attention to: grant applications submitted (and re-submitted), symposia organized, spaces and classes created, leadership and service to the department and academic community, leadership to and education of the community outside of academia, creation of public policy and impact on public health, and participation in public relations or recruiting efforts.
evidence: Authors' recommendation for what to include in letters

claim: Many achievements should be framed as scholarship rather than service because they reflect the scholar's standing in the field.
source: When possible, frame this as scholarship rather than service, because many of these achievements reflect the scholar's standing in the field.
evidence: Authors' recommendation for framing accomplishments

claim: Letter writers should recognize explicitly the candidate's experiences and characteristics that bring wisdom and perspective beyond chronological years and official titles.
source: For Black and other historically marginalized scholars in particular, recognize explicitly the candidate's experiences and characteristics that bring wisdom and perspective beyond chronological years and official titles (Figure 1 middle, box 4).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Life experiences and identity characteristics provide unique perspectives that enhance the academic environment.
source: Those life experiences and identity characteristics (such as engaging in outreach programs, being an immigrant or international scholar, coming from a disadvantaged, under-resourced, or other path that has been historically underrepresented in academia) provide unique perspectives that enhance their environment.
evidence: Authors' assertion about the value of diverse perspectives

claim: Mentoring is often disproportionately done by Black and other historically marginalized scholars.
source: An important aspect of contribution to scholarly work and discourse is mentoring, which is often disproportionately done by Black and other historically marginalized scholars.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about service burdens

claim: Letter writers should elaborate on the candidate's mentorship, including the number of mentees and the contributions and successes of the candidate's mentees and advisees.
source: In your letter, elaborate on the candidate's mentorship (Figure 1 middle, box 5): include the number of mentees (direct and indirect) that rely on the candidate for support and note the contributions and successes of the candidate's mentees and advisees.
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Letter writers should add literature-supported encouragement for evaluators to account for systemic racism in academia.
source: We encourage you to add literature-supported encouragement for evaluators to account for systemic racism in academia (Figure 1 middle, box 6).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: There are known racial disparities in grant funding.
source: For example, you can include "Given the known racial disparities in grant funding (Taffe and Gilpin, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Taffe and Gilpin, 2021

claim: There are known racial disparities in publication rates.
source: and publication rates (Lerback et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lerback et al., 2020

claim: There is epistemic exclusion of minoritized faculty.
source: and the epistemic exclusion of minoritized faculty (Settles et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Settles et al., 2022

claim: Achievement in spite of systemic barriers enhances the value of the scholar's accomplishments.
source: We recommend emphasizing that achievement in spite of the systemic barriers enhances the value of the scholar's accomplishments rather than offering such barriers as a rationale for any potential perceived weaknesses.
evidence: Authors' recommendation for framing barriers

claim: Letter writers should avoid reductive comparisons to an arbitrary standard, a model/prototype, or a scholar at another institution.
source: We recommend you avoid (and ignore requests for) reductive comparisons to an arbitrary standard, a model/prototype, or a scholar at another institution (Figure 1 middle, box 7).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Comparisons cannot account for the varied intersecting identities and experiences of different scholars.
source: Such comparisons cannot account for the varied intersecting identities and experiences of different scholars.
evidence: Authors' reasoning for avoiding comparisons

claim: The anti-racist approach to letter-writing is not about diluting the quality of tenured faculty or lowering the bar for promotion.
source: This approach is not about diluting the quality of tenured faculty or lowering the bar for promotion, but rather critiquing the devaluation of many types of scholarly contributions and recognizing the importance of such work both to the scholar's institution and to their field of study.
evidence: Authors' clarification of their goals

claim: Letter writers should cite the scholar in their own work wherever appropriate after writing the letter.
source: First, now that you are familiar with the work of this scholar in your field, make sure to cite them in your own work wherever appropriate (Figure 1 bottom, box 1).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Racial disparities in whose work is cited persist across a variety of disciplines.
source: Racial disparities in whose work is cited persist across a variety of disciplines (Ray, 2018; Shirani, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on citation disparities

claim: Letter writers can reach out to the candidate to convey appreciation of their scholarly work and offer specific support or mentorship.
source: As you might do for junior scholars you already know well, you can also reach out to the candidate to convey your appreciation of their scholarly work and offer specific support or mentorship, such as inviting them to give a talk at your department (Figure 1 bottom, box 2).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Letter writers can support the candidate through sponsorship and nominations.
source: Regardless of whether you connect directly, you can support the candidate through sponsorship and nominations (Figure 1 bottom, box 3).
evidence: Authors' recommendation with reference to Figure 1

claim: Actions by letter writers will serve to educate colleagues on the scholarship of the candidate and on similar types of work they may be unfamiliar with.
source: These actions on your part will not only benefit the scholar, they will also serve to educate your colleagues on the scholarship of this particular person, and on similar types of work they may be unfamiliar with (and might be called upon to evaluate in tenure and promotion letters in the future).
evidence: Authors' inference about the broader impact of their recommendations

claim: Letter writers should consider expanding their anti-racism work by advocating for changes to the promotion criteria at their own institution.
source: Additionally, after following these suggestions for writing anti-racist tenure letters, consider expanding your anti-racism work by advocating for changes to the promotion criteria at your own institution drawing on the considerations outlined here.
evidence: Authors' recommendation for broader advocacy

claim: A list of letter writers who have committed to using these guidelines will serve as a public resource for candidates and universities.
source: Finally, as an intentionally anti-racist letter writer, we hope you will join a list of letter writers who have committed to using these guidelines (to join, fill in this form: https://forms.gle/4F4hBb9MNsrwdEDz6). This list (bit.ly/TenureEquity) will serve as a public resource for candidates and universities looking for anti-racist letter-writers.
evidence: Authors' description of a resource they have created

claim: Many early-career scholars who are marginalized in their field do not have a 'natural' mentoring and support network.
source: Many early-career scholars who are marginalized in their field do not have a 'natural' mentoring and support network and could benefit from proactive acknowledgment and support.
evidence: Authors' inference about the needs of marginalized scholars

claim: The guidance is based on current best understanding of the nature of 'white supremacy culture' in academia and how to counteract it within the tenure recommendation letter.
source: The guidance we provided above is based on our current best understanding of the nature of 'white supremacy culture' in academia and how to counteract it within the tenure recommendation letter.
evidence: Authors' statement about the basis of their guidance

claim: The process is based on strong theoretical foundations and shaped by the input of a diverse range of scholars and the leadership of the Academics for Black Survival and Wellness organization.
source: While our process is based on strong theoretical foundations (Okun, 2021) and shaped by the input of a diverse range of scholars and the leadership of the Academics for Black Survival and Wellness organization
evidence: Authors' statement about the development of their recommendations

claim: The guidelines cannot perfectly apply to all situations and will need revision and reimagining over time.
source: these guidelines cannot perfectly apply to all situations and will need revision and reimagining over time.
evidence: Authors' acknowledgment of the limitations of their guidelines

claim: The role of an external evaluator for a tenure candidate is one in which faculty have substantial freedom to adopt an anti-racist approach.
source: We recognize that the role of an external evaluator for a tenure candidate is one in which faculty have substantial freedom to adopt an anti-racist approach.
evidence: Authors' observation about the opportunities for anti-racist action

claim: Anti-racist tenure letters may be met with resistance and even backlash by tenure committees.
source: To be sure, anti-racist tenure letters may be met with resistance and even backlash by tenure committees, as many academics are (implicitly) committed to maintaining power structures that are familiar to them, and that confer them with outsized power and privilege.
evidence: Authors' speculation about potential resistance

claim: Many academics are implicitly committed to maintaining power structures that are familiar to them and that confer them with outsized power and privilege.
source: as many academics are (implicitly) committed to maintaining power structures that are familiar to them, and that confer them with outsized power and privilege.
evidence: Authors' inference about academic culture

claim: Letter writers should directly rebut what might traditionally be considered 'weaknesses' in the applicant's file by explicitly addressing why they do not consider these as weaknesses.
source: We suggest to directly rebut, in your letter, what might traditionally be considered 'weaknesses' in the applicant's file, by explicitly addressing why you do not consider these as weaknesses.
evidence: Authors' recommendation for addressing potential resistance

claim: Resistance-anticipating arguments will provide much needed ammunition for other advocates involved in the tenure process at the candidate's home institution.
source: Such resistance-anticipating arguments will provide much needed ammunition for other advocates involved in the tenure process at the candidate's home institution.
evidence: Authors' inference about the strategic value of their recommendations

claim: The suggestions cannot ameliorate the persistent opportunity gaps and discrimination that Black scholars face in their educational and professional careers.
source: Unfortunately, our suggestions cannot ameliorate the persistent opportunity gaps and discrimination that Black scholars face in their educational and professional careers.
evidence: Authors' acknowledgment of the limitations of their recommendations

claim: Resistance to white supremacy culture must be accompanied by systemic reforms.
source: We offer these recommendations as one avenue for resisting 'white supremacy culture' in academia with the understanding that such resistance must be accompanied by systemic reforms.
evidence: Authors' assertion about the need for broader change

claim: Some institutions are introducing diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) requirements for tenure or forging new DEI-focused pathways to tenure.
source: Even as some institutions introduce diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) requirements for tenure or forge new DEI-focused pathways to tenure
evidence: Based on knowledge about current institutional changes

claim: The success of DEI projects in creating an inclusive and equitable academic culture will require openly acknowledging racism in academia.
source: the success of such projects in creating an inclusive and equitable academic culture will require openly acknowledging racism in academia (Gosztyla et al., 2021)
evidence: Authors' assertion with supporting citation

claim: Creating an inclusive and equitable academic culture requires taking a proactive approach to an inclusive workplace culture and retaining Black scholars.
source: taking a proactive approach to an inclusive workplace culture and retaining Black scholars (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to National Academies report

claim: Creating an inclusive and equitable academic culture requires introducing changes to tenure evaluation policies and practices.
source: and introducing changes to tenure evaluation policies (e.g. recognizing the myriad biases in student evaluations of teaching) and practices (e.g, nomination and selection of letter writers, instructions provided to letter writers, how evaluators are trained).
evidence: Authors' recommendations for systemic changes
